name: null-list?
summary: True when a list argument is empty -- like null?, but it asserts that the argument really was a list.
explanation: null? is a question about any object: is this the empty list? null-list? is a question about a list: are you at the end of it? The difference looks like nothing and matters at exactly one moment -- when your loop has walked off the end of a structure that was never a proper list to begin with. Given a dotted list, a cdr-walk eventually lands on the improper tail, and null? calmly answers #f, so the loop takes another cdr and raises somewhere deeper, in a frame that tells you nothing about the real mistake. null-list? is the version that says the argument was supposed to be a list and this is not one. It is the contract made explicit at the point where the contract is actually consumed. Use null? when you are classifying an unknown object; use null-list? when you have promised yourself you are holding a list and want that promise checked.

examples.note: (#t #f) -- on ordinary lists it answers exactly what null? would.

examples.code:
(define (count-down xs n)
  (if (null-list? xs) n (count-down (cdr xs) (+ n 1))))
(display (list 'three (count-down '(a b c) 0)
               'empty (count-down '() 0)
               'one (count-down '(z) 0)))
(newline)
examples.note: (three 3 empty 0 one 1) -- as a loop terminator it reads as "am I at the end", which is what the loop means.
(proper done guarded refused) -- the improper case is turned away before the walk starts, which is the discipline null-list? is asking for.

caveats: On every proper list it is indistinguishable from null?. The whole point is the case where the argument is NOT a proper list.
It is not a general classifier. Do not use it to ask whether an arbitrary object is the empty list -- that is null?, and it accepts anything.
It does not walk the list. It looks at the object in front of it, so it is O(1); it is not a proper-list? check in disguise.
Checking the whole list up front with proper-list? costs a full walk. null-list? at each step costs nothing extra, which is why it belongs in the loop rather than before it.
A dotted list is still improper even if you never reach its tail. Stopping early on a predicate means the check never fires, and the bug stays latent.
usecases: The termination test of a hand-written cdr-walk, where it documents that a list was expected.
Recursive list procedures whose base case should be reached rather than fallen past.
Replacing null? in library code, where the argument came from a caller and the contract deserves stating.

learn.concept: Two predicates can agree on every value you have tried and still mean different things -- the difference is what they assert about their argument.
learn.progression: Write a cdr-walk with null? and it works. Feed it (1 . 2) and watch the error surface two frames too deep. Switch to null-list? and the intent is documented at the point of use. Then learn that the real fix is often to check proper-list? once at the boundary -- and that null-list? is what you use inside once you have.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (batch-total prices)
  (let loop ((rest prices) (sum 0))
    (if (null-list? rest) sum (loop (cdr rest) (+ sum (car rest))))))
(display (list 'cart (batch-total '(499 250 1200))
               'empty (batch-total '())
               'single (batch-total '(75))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (walk-guarded xs)
  (if (proper-list? xs)
      (let loop ((r xs) (n 0)) (if (null-list? r) n (loop (cdr r) (+ n 1))))
      'improper))
(display (map walk-guarded (list '(a b c) '() (cons 'a 'b) '(a . b))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A checkout routine sums a list of line-item prices supplied by a caller. Candidates: null-list? (O(1) per step, terminates the loop, and states in the code that a list was the contract), null? (identical on good input, but on a dotted list it silently answers #f and the failure surfaces one cdr later as a car error on a number), pair? as the CONTINUE test (works and is arguably safer, but it stops silently on an improper tail instead of complaining, hiding the caller's bug), proper-list? checked every iteration (correct and quadratic -- a full walk per step), length compared against an index (a walk up front plus index arithmetic, and it raises on improper input before you can report anything useful). null-list? is the pick because the loop is already stepping and the assertion is free.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a cart total over three prices, an empty cart, and a single item -- the three shapes any accumulator loop has to get right. math: a product where the base case returns the multiplicative identity, over a three-element list, an empty one, and a singleton. cs: the guarded form, where proper-list? is paid once at the boundary and null-list? runs inside, so both improper inputs are turned away by name rather than by crash.
row-2-audit.meta: The cs program is the honest pattern and the other two are the common one. Checking proper-list? once outside the loop is O(n) and makes every step inside safe; checking it inside would be O(n^2) for the same guarantee.
row-2-audit.eng: An empty cart must total zero, not raise. The base case of an accumulator is the identity of its operation, and that is a design decision worth writing down.
row-2-audit.math: The empty product is 1 for the same reason the empty sum is 0: the base case must be the identity element or folding loses associativity.
row-2-audit.cs: Validate at the boundary, assert in the loop. Paying O(n) once buys you O(1) safety at every step, which is why proper-list? and null-list? are complements rather than competitors.

row-3-dimension.setup: Asking, at each step of a walk, whether there is anything left.

rungs.domain: a sensor feed being drained until it runs dry, with the last reading held
rungs.code:
(define (final-reading feed fallback)
  (let loop ((f feed) (last fallback) (n 0))
    (if (null-list? f)
        (list 'last last 'samples n)
        (loop (cdr f) (car f) (+ n 1)))))
(display (list (final-reading '(21 22 24 23) 'none)
               (final-reading '() 'none)
               (final-reading '(19) 'none)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a parser consuming a token stream and refusing to run past the end
rungs.code:
(define (parse-pairs toks)
  (let loop ((t toks) (acc '()))
    (cond ((null-list? t) (list 'ok (reverse acc)))
          ((null-list? (cdr t)) (list 'dangling (car t) 'so-far (reverse acc)))
          (else (loop (cddr t) (cons (cons (car t) (cadr t)) acc))))))
(display (list (parse-pairs '(a 1 b 2))
               (parse-pairs '(a 1 b))
               (parse-pairs '())))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare lists it is a yes-or-no about emptiness and nothing else. On a sensor feed the predicate is what ENDS an accumulation that carries state -- the loop is keeping the previous element and a count, so reaching the end is the moment those get reported rather than discarded, and the empty feed must produce the fallback instead of an error. In the parser the same predicate is called twice per iteration on two different objects: once on the stream to detect the clean end, and once on its cdr to detect an odd-length stream, which is a lookahead. That second call is the one that turns a crash into a diagnosis. The verb never changes; what climbs is how much of the program's correctness rests on asking at the right moment.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rung three is the only one where null-list? appears twice, and the two calls mean different things -- end of input versus insufficient input. A parser that only checked the first would take (cadr t) of a one-element list and raise.
row-3-dimension.eng: A drain loop that must survive an empty feed needs its fallback decided before the loop, not discovered inside it.
row-3-dimension.math: Consuming two elements per step partitions a list by parity. The odd case is not an error in the data, it is a case in the function, and it has to be written.
row-3-dimension.cs: Lookahead is checking emptiness of the tail before dereferencing it. Every recursive-descent parser is that check repeated at each production.

row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (end-is-reached-once? xs)
  (let loop ((r xs) (n 0))
    (if (null-list? r)
        (= n (length xs))
        (loop (cdr r) (+ n 1)))))
(display (map end-is-reached-once? '(() (1) (1 2) (a b c d) (() ()))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (complementary-with-pair? xs)
  (let ((e (null-list? xs)) (p (pair? xs)))
    (and (or e p) (not (and e p)))))
(display (map complementary-with-pair? (list '() '(1) '(1 2) (list 'a) (list))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: On any proper list null-list? agrees with null? exactly; a cdr-walk terminated by null-list? takes precisely as many steps as the list is long; and on a proper list null-list? and pair? are complements, so the walk has exactly two states and no third.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all proper lists xs, null-list?(xs) = null?(xs); the cdr-walk stopping at null-list? performs |xs| steps; and exactly one of null-list?(xs) and pair?(xs) holds
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: agreement with the general predicate, exact step count, and the two-state property that makes the walk total. What would falsify them: a disagreement on some proper list, a walk that stopped early or late, or a list that answered #f to both -- which is what an improper tail would do, and is precisely the case null-list? exists to catch. The empty list is in all three because it is where the loop body never runs.
row-4-proof.eng: The agreement law is what makes null-list? a drop-in replacement for null? in list code. If it were not, every substitution would need review.
row-4-proof.math: Step count equal to length is the statement that the walk is a bijection onto the indices. It is the induction hypothesis every list proof is built on.
row-4-proof.cs: Two mutually exclusive, jointly exhaustive states is what makes a loop total. A third state -- neither empty nor a pair -- is exactly an improper tail, and it is a runtime error rather than a branch.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (done? rest) (null-list? rest))
(define (chunk xs size)
  (let loop ((r xs) (out '()))
    (if (done? r)
        (reverse out)
        (let inner ((r2 r) (k size) (part '()))
          (if (or (= k 0) (done? r2))
              (loop r2 (cons (reverse part) out))
              (inner (cdr r2) (- k 1) (cons (car r2) part)))))))
(display (list 'even (chunk '(1 2 3 4 5 6) 2)
               'ragged (chunk '(a b c d e) 3)
               'empty (chunk '() 4)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (at-end? xs) (null-list? xs))
(define (running-sums xs)
  (let loop ((r xs) (acc 0) (out '()))
    (if (at-end? r)
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr r) (+ acc (car r)) (cons (+ acc (car r)) out)))))
(display (list 'partials (running-sums '(1 2 3 4))
               'total (let ((p (running-sums '(5 5 5)))) (if (null-list? p) 0 (car (reverse p))))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (exhausted? s) (null-list? s))
(define (run-length s)
  (let loop ((r s) (out '()))
    (if (exhausted? r)
        (reverse out)
        (let inner ((r2 (cdr r)) (n 1))
          (if (or (exhausted? r2) (not (eqv? (car r2) (car r))))
              (loop r2 (cons (cons (car r) n) out))
              (inner (cdr r2) (+ n 1)))))))
(display (list (run-length '(a a b c c c))
               (run-length '(x))
               (run-length '())))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: null-list? answers whether a walk over a list has anything left to consume.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: done? is one call; chunk uses it in TWO nested loops -- the outer one to know when the whole list is finished, the inner one to close a short final group -- and ragged chunking falls out with no length arithmetic. math: at-end? is one call; running-sums turns a list into its prefix sums in one pass, and the total is then the last partial rather than a second traversal. cs: exhausted? is one call; run-length compresses a sequence into (value . count) pairs, and the inner loop's use of the helper is what stops the final run from reading past the end.
row-5-emergence.meta: Each composition calls its helper from an inner loop as well as an outer one, and in every case the inner call is the one guarding a car or cdr that would otherwise raise. That is the whole argument for naming the predicate: the interesting uses are not the loop terminator, they are the lookaheads.
row-5-emergence.eng: Chunking with a ragged tail is where every hand-rolled batcher goes wrong. Deciding emptiness rather than computing remaining length makes the short last group automatic.
row-5-emergence.math: Prefix sums are a scan, and a scan is a fold that keeps its intermediate states. One pass produces both the sequence and its total.
row-5-emergence.cs: Run-length encoding is the simplest compressor there is, and its only subtlety is the boundary -- a run that ends because the stream ended, not because the value changed.
